title: Security Zones, Placement, and Attack Surface

blocks.text: A well-chosen control placed in the wrong spot protects nothing. The exam tests your ability to say **where** to put each control, **what traffic** passes through it, and **what happens if it fails**.

A secure architecture divides the network into zones of decreasing trust. Traffic flows from an **untrusted** zone (Internet) through a **buffer zone** (DMZ) before reaching the **internal** zone. Every crossing is a checkpoint.

Objective

blocks.field: Placement determines which packets a control sees. An IDS placed out-of-path will not see traffic; a control placed after the flaw cannot prevent it.

blocks.text: Exam rule: a **preventive** control must be **in the path** of traffic (inline); a **detective** control can be **out-of-path** (SPAN/tap).

blocks.field: Set of points through which an attacker can interact with a system: open ports, exposed services, accounts, APIs, interfaces. The fewer there are, the fewer targets exist.
Using different vendors, systems, and mechanisms so that a single flaw or outage does not affect the entire infrastructure.

blocks.note: Knowing what you are protecting and why: inventory and criticality

left.title: Fail-Open
points: If the control fails, traffic passes.
Risk: silent bypass of the control.

right.title: Fail-Closed
points: If the control fails, traffic is blocked.

blocks.note: Failure mode decisions for network controls

blocks.text: A scenario saying "the service must remain available even if authentication fails" expects **fail-open**. A scenario "never allow unauthenticated access" expects **fail-closed**.

blocks.q: An intrusion sensor must see all traffic on a segment without being able to block it. Where should it be placed?
options: In the DMZ after the firewall, in blocking mode
blocks.explain: An IDS is detective: a mirror port or tap gives it a copy of traffic without interrupting it. An IPS would be placed inline.

items: DMZ = buffer zone between the Internet and the internal network.
A preventive control is inline; a detective control can be out-of-path.
Reducing the attack surface means closing unnecessary ports, services, and accounts.
Fail-open prioritizes availability; fail-closed prioritizes security.

title: Zero Trust, Remote Access, and Service Identities

blocks.text: The **Zero Trust** model replaces implicit trust tied to network location with continuous verification: **never trust, always verify**. The exam expects you to know which signals to verify before granting access.

blocks.note: Zero Trust: identity, device, inventory, and application access control

items.title: User authentication
items.text: Verify the user's identity (MFA, federation), not just their presence on a network.

items.title: Device health
items.text: Check device state: patches up to date, active antivirus, encryption, compliant posture.

items.title: Device inventory
items.text: Verify that the device is known and inventoried; an unknown device is denied or quarantined.

items.title: Application access control
items.text: Grant minimal rights to the requested resource, session by session, with continuous re-evaluation.

blocks.field: Model where no user, device, or traffic flow is trusted by default, even inside the network. Access is granted after verifying identity, device health, and inventory.

blocks.text: Remote Access, Tunneling, and Out-of-Band Management

blocks.field: Encrypts traffic between a remote user and the internal network. It authenticates the tunnel, not automatically each application.

items: **Remote access**: remote user access with MFA and posture checking.
**Tunneling**: encrypted encapsulation of traffic between two endpoints.
**End-to-end encrypted messaging**: end-to-end encryption of communications.
**File transfer**: dedicated, logged channel with content inspection.
**Out-of-band management**: separate administration network; the **bastion** (jump host) is its single entry point, with MFA and recorded sessions.

blocks.text: SSE and Group Managed Service Accounts

blocks.field: Set of security services delivered from the cloud near users (proxy, web filtering, DLP, access control) to replace or complement the enterprise VPN.
Service account whose password is automatically managed by the directory and rotated without manual intervention: it avoids hardcoded passwords and forgotten service accounts.

blocks.note: Official objectives — SSE and gMSA absent from the 4 books

blocks.text: SSE and gMSA are required in **§3.2** but do not appear in any of the four provided books. The definitions above come from the objectives and industry practice.

**Privilege creep** occurs when a user accumulates rights across role changes without old rights being removed. The fix: **least privilege** accounts, periodic access reviews, and controlled emergency accounts.

blocks.note: Access control, privileges, and rights review

blocks.q: An uninventoried personal device requests access to an internal application. What should a Zero Trust architecture do?
options: Allow because the user is authenticated
Deny or quarantine until device inventory and health are verified
Defer the decision to the VPN provider
blocks.explain: Zero Trust verifies the user AND the device (health + inventory) before granting minimal application access.

items: Zero Trust = verify user, device health, inventory, and application access.
Bastion and out-of-band management isolate administration from the user network.
SSE and gMSA are objectives concepts absent from the books.
Counter privilege creep with least privilege and access reviews.
